# Piston Origins

> Piston Origins is a car-history YouTube channel telling the origin stories of legendary cars: JDM icons like the Toyota Supra, Nissan Skyline GT-R, Mazda RX-7, Honda NSX and AE86, the engines behind them (2JZ, RB26, rotary, 4A-GE) and the rivalries, bans and comebacks that made them. A new full car story every week, plus 60-second car secrets in Shorts, with every source listed.

Piston Origins is on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/@PistonOrigins and Instagram at https://www.instagram.com/pistonorigins/. The host (Skye) and narration voice are AI-generated; the research, facts and sources are real and listed in every video description and on each episode page below.

## Episodes (full car stories)

- [Ferrari vs Lamborghini: How a Broken Clutch Started a Rivalry](https://pistonorigins.com/episodes/ferrari-vs-lamborghini-origin-story/): How tractor maker Ferruccio Lamborghini took on Enzo Ferrari: the clutch row, the engineless 350 GTV, the Miura, the Countach and losing his company.
- [Nissan GT-R vs Porsche 911 Turbo: 2008 Nürburgring Dispute](https://pistonorigins.com/episodes/nissan-gt-r-vs-porsche-911-turbo-nurburgring/): In 2008 Porsche bought a Nissan GT-R R35, lapped the Nürburgring in 7:54 against Nissan's claimed 7:29 and suggested race tyres. Here is how Nissan answered.
- [Lexus LFA History: The V10 Supercar Toyota Lost Money On](https://pistonorigins.com/episodes/lexus-lfa-story/): Lexus LFA history: the Yamaha-built 4.8-litre V10, the switch from aluminium to carbon fibre, the Nürburgring, and why Toyota lost money on all 500 cars.

- [Mazda Rotary Engine History: RX-7, 787B and the Le Mans Win](https://pistonorigins.com/episodes/mazda-rotary-engine-rx-7-787b-story/): Mazda rotary engine history, from the 1961 NSU Wankel licence and the devil's nail marks to the RX-7, the 787B's 1991 Le Mans win and the 2023 comeback.

- [Toyota Supra Mk4 (A80) History: The 2JZ and How It Was Built](https://pistonorigins.com/episodes/toyota-supra-mk4-story/): Toyota Supra Mk4 (A80) history: from the 2000GT and Celica Supra to Isao Tsuzuki's "less is more" design, the 2JZ-GTE sequential twin-turbo and its legacy.

## EP 09: Toyota Cheated So Well, the FIA Called It Genius

URL: https://pistonorigins.com/episodes/toyota-celica-gt-four-1995-wrc-turbo-restrictor/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OHUYDjP9DVQ
Published: 2026-10-27 · Length: 5:43 · Subject: Toyota Celica GT-Four ST205

How Toyota Team Europe hid an illegal turbo restrictor in the 1995 World Rally Championship, in the Celica GT-Four ST205, and why FIA president Max Mosley called it genius. Toyota was leading both world championships with two rallies left. Then scrutineers at Rally Catalunya took Auriol's car apart.

### Key facts

- Car: Toyota Celica GT-Four (ST205)
- Engine: 3S-GTE 2.0 L turbo inline-four
- Team: Toyota Team Europe
- Season: 1995 World Rally Championship
- Where it unravelled: Rally Catalunya, October 1995

### The story

#### Toyota Team Europe and the Celica GT-Four

In 1995 Toyota was not the underdog of the World Rally Championship. It was the team everyone else was chasing. Its rally operation was not even run from Japan: it worked out of Cologne in Germany as Toyota Team Europe, and its weapon was the Celica GT-Four, a turbocharged, four-wheel-drive car built for mud, snow and gravel.

The record behind it was formidable. In 1990 Carlos Sainz won the drivers' world title in a Celica GT-Four, the first time a Japanese car had done it. In 1993 Toyota became the first Japanese manufacturer to win the world title, and in 1994 it won again. By 1995 the latest car, the Celica GT-Four ST205 with its 2.0-litre 3S-GTE turbo four, was carrying the weight of all that success.


#### The 1995 WRC turbo restrictor rule

That season the rule book had one job: slow these cars down. Every turbo engine had to breathe through a restrictor, a metal ring with a small hole placed right in front of the turbocharger. The effect is like making a sprinter run while breathing through a straw. Less air means less power, and the limit worked out at about 300 horsepower. Every car was checked.

On paper, the new Celica was struggling. It had won just one rally all year, in Corsica. And yet, with two rounds left, Toyota was leading both world championships.


#### Suspicion at Rally Australia

The first public doubts surfaced at Rally Australia, on a short show stage in a park in Perth where two cars race side by side. Rivals watched the Celicas leave the line and pull away from the Subarus. Juha Kankkunen's co-driver, Nicky Grist, later suggested that was the mistake: showing that kind of speed on live television. People started asking questions.


#### Rally Catalunya, October 1995

The next round was Rally Catalunya in Spain, round seven of eight. Kankkunen, already a four-time world champion, took the lead on stage two and built a gap of almost a minute. Then, on day two, he found a left-hander tighter than he expected, ran out of road and rolled the Celica out of the rally. Team-mate Didier Auriol kept going and finished fourth, so Toyota's title hopes were still alive.

Then the scrutineers took Auriol's car apart. They pulled off a hose and checked the turbo, and everything looked legal. Hours later, Auriol was thrown out: his turbo restrictor did not match the rule book.


#### How the turbo restrictor cheat worked

The restrictor itself was perfectly legal. Remove it, measure it, and it passed. The trick was hidden in the air hose around it. Inside was a flange held shut by a strong spring. When mechanics clamped the hose in place, the clips forced that flange open by just 5 mm.

Five millimetres sounds trivial, but it let air sneak around the restrictor and straight into the turbo. That was roughly 25 per cent more air, worth up to 50 extra horsepower on cars meant to be limited to 300.

The clever part was what happened under inspection. The moment an inspector undid the clips to check the system, the spring snapped the flange shut, and the evidence erased itself. Even the springs were polished and machined so they would not disturb the airflow, and opening the device again needed a special tool. The diagrams usually used to explain it are simplified, but the principle is that simple: a legal part, bypassed by a hose that only cheated while it was fitted to the car.


#### The FIA ban: Toyota excluded from the 1995 championship

On 3 November 1995 the FIA's World Motor Sport Council met in an emergency session. Toyota Team Europe was excluded from the 1995 championship and every point erased. Kankkunen, Auriol and Armin Schwarz lost everything they had scored, and the team was banned for 12 months, covering the whole of the 1996 season.

With Toyota gone, the drivers' title went to a 27-year-old Scot in a blue Subaru, Colin McRae, and Subaru took the manufacturers' title too.

The most surprising reaction came from the man who handed down the punishment. FIA president Max Mosley described the device as the most ingenious thing he had seen in 30 years of motorsport, and called the parts inside "beautifully made". He also said there was nothing to suggest the drivers knew. Toyota's position was that the device had been made at a certain level of the team without management knowing. The FIA's answer was blunt: a team is responsible for everything it does.

Some questions remain open. Who designed the device has never been publicly named, and even how the FIA found it is still debated.


#### Toyota's WRC comeback

The ban was not the end of Toyota in rallying. In 1999 its Corolla WRC won the manufacturers' world title. Toyota later left the sport, then returned in 2017 with the Yaris. As of 2026 it holds 10 manufacturers' titles, level with Lancia for the most in the championship's history.

That is the strange arc of this story: the team behind the cleverest cheat rallying has seen went on to become one of the most successful it has ever had. Whether the Celica ST205's hidden hose was genius or simply cheating is still the argument it was in 1995.


### Questions and answers

**Why was Toyota banned from the 1995 World Rally Championship?**
At Rally Catalunya in October 1995, scrutineers took apart Didier Auriol's Toyota Celica GT-Four ST205 and found that Toyota Team Europe had engineered a way around the mandatory turbo restrictor, letting the engine breathe more air than the rules allowed. Toyota was excluded from the 1995 championship.

**What did the FIA say about Toyota's turbo cheat?**
FIA president Max Mosley famously praised its ingenuity, calling it the most ingenious thing he had seen in motorsport, even as the team was punished.

## EP 08: Ferrari vs Lamborghini: The Insult That Started It All

URL: https://pistonorigins.com/episodes/ferrari-vs-lamborghini-origin-story/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YPdVXp1ca0c
Published: 2026-10-24 · Length: 7:44 · Subject: Lamborghini 350 GT and Miura

Ferruccio Lamborghini was a tractor maker who drove Ferraris. When the clutch kept failing, he went to Maranello to complain, and Enzo Ferrari supposedly told him he'd never handle a Ferrari. This is the full Lamborghini vs Ferrari origin story. He built a V12 rival in four months, showed a car with no engine, then shocked the world with the Miura, the car that invented the supercar. Was the insult real, or a story Ferruccio liked to tell? And who actually won: Ferrari or Lamborghini?

### Key facts

- Founder: Ferruccio Lamborghini (born 1916, near Cento)
- Before cars: Lamborghini Trattori, founded 1948
- Company founded: 30 October 1963, Sant'Agata Bolognese
- First show car: 350 GTV, Turin 1963, shown without an engine
- Breakthrough: Miura (chassis Turin 1965, car Geneva 1966)

### The story

#### Ferruccio Lamborghini, the tractor maker

Ferruccio Lamborghini was born in 1916 on a farm near Cento in northern Italy, and from the start he cared more about the machines than the fields. During the Second World War he served as an air force mechanic on the island of Rhodes, running the unit that kept the vehicles going.

When the war ended, Italy was full of abandoned military vehicles. In 1948 Ferruccio began turning them into tractors, and because farmers needed them, Lamborghini Trattori boomed. In 1959 he added a second business making oil burners, then moved into air conditioning, and he became very rich.


#### The Ferrari clutch problem

Rich Italians of the period bought Ferraris, and Ferruccio was no exception. He owned a Ferrari 250 GT coupé, then a 250 GT SWB Berlinetta, then a 250 GT 2+2. One thing kept going wrong on them: the clutch. Again and again his cars went back to Maranello to be rebuilt.

When Ferruccio looked inside, the story goes, he found that the clutch parts were essentially the same ones he was already using in his tractors. That was what made him angry enough to ask to see Enzo Ferrari himself.


#### Did Enzo Ferrari really insult Lamborghini?

The famous exchange comes from Ferruccio's own account, given in a 1991 interview. As he told it, he said to Enzo that his cars were rubbish, and Enzo replied that Lamborghini might be able to drive a tractor but would never be able to handle a Ferrari properly.

Not everyone close to the company has accepted that version. Lamborghini's long-serving test driver Valentino Balboni believes it. His predecessor, Bob Wallace, doubted it. The historian Massimo Delbo put it neatly: something was said, but only Enzo and Ferruccio knew what.

Ferruccio's biographer offers a more practical explanation. If tractor-grade parts were going into expensive sports cars, the profit on each one had to be enormous, and a businessman would notice that. Insult or business opportunity? Probably both.


#### Automobili Lamborghini and the 350 GTV with no engine

Automobili Lamborghini was founded on 30 October 1963, with a brand-new factory at Sant'Agata Bolognese, a short drive from Ferrari. To design the engine, Ferruccio hired Giotto Bizzarrini, who had left Ferrari two years earlier. Bizzarrini produced a V12 so extreme it was essentially a racing engine, which was not what Ferruccio wanted for a comfortable grand tourer. The two argued, and Ferruccio refused to pay his fee.

That same month the first Lamborghini, the 350 GTV, appeared at the Turin Motor Show. It had one problem: there was no engine in it. The finished production car, the 350 GT, arrived at Geneva in 1964, and 120 were built. Respectable, but hardly a Ferrari killer.


#### The Lamborghini Miura: the car that invented the supercar

The breakthrough came from three young men, all in their mid-twenties: engineer Gian Paolo Dallara, designer Marcello Gandini and test driver Bob Wallace. Their idea was to take the V12, turn it sideways and mount it behind the driver.

In 1965 Lamborghini showed only the bare chassis at Turin. Then, in March 1966 at Geneva, the complete Miura was revealed: low, wide and startlingly beautiful. It was the fastest production car in the world, capable of close to 280 km/h, and Lamborghini went on to build just over 750 of them. Today it is widely called the car that invented the supercar, and it came from a company whose founder made tractors.


#### Why Lamborghini uses a raging bull

The name has its own origin. In 1962 Ferruccio visited the ranch of Don Eduardo Miura near Seville, home of some of Spain's fiercest fighting bulls, and he loved them. He was also a Taurus. So when he started his car company, he put a raging bull on the badge, and the Miura was named after those bulls.

It began a tradition. Espada means a matador's sword, and Islero, Diablo and Murciélago are all names linked to fighting bulls. Ferrari had its prancing horse; Lamborghini had its bull.


#### How Ferrari responded to the mid-engined Miura

Enzo Ferrari, the man who reportedly said Ferruccio could not handle a Ferrari, believed a mid-engined road car would be too difficult for ordinary customers to drive. His own engineers needed years to convince him otherwise. Ferrari's first mid-engined 12-cylinder road car, the Berlinetta Boxer, did not arrive until 1973, seven years after the Miura.

Lamborghini kept moving. In 1968 came the Espada, a four-seat supercar, of which 1,227 were built. In 1971 the Countach prototype appeared at Geneva. Its name comes from a word in the Piedmontese dialect, a shout of amazement, and the story goes that it was exactly what Nuccio Bertone said when he first saw the car. Production began in 1974, and the Countach became the poster on a generation of bedroom walls.


#### How Ferruccio lost Lamborghini

While the cars grew wilder, Ferruccio's business grew harder. In 1972 he sold his tractor company and, in the same year, 51 per cent of the car company. In 1974 he sold the rest and walked away, retiring to a farm on Lake Trasimeno where he made wine.

Without him, Automobili Lamborghini went bankrupt in 1978. It was bought for $3 million in 1980, by Chrysler in 1987 for about $25 million, and by Audi in 1998 for about $110 million. Ferruccio Lamborghini died in 1993, five years before the Audi sale, so he never saw what his company became.

The numbers today show how close the rivalry has become. In 2025 Lamborghini delivered a record 10,747 cars, while Ferrari shipped 13,640. Ferrari is still bigger, but the company that, by its founder's account, began with a failing clutch and a sharp remark is now right behind it.


### Questions and answers

**Why did Ferruccio Lamborghini start making cars?**
Ferruccio Lamborghini was a tractor maker who owned Ferraris. When the clutch kept failing he complained to Enzo Ferrari, who, as Ferruccio told the story, said a tractor maker could never handle a Ferrari. Ferruccio decided to build his own grand tourer. His biographer argues the real motive was economic: there was money in high-end cars.

**Was Lamborghini's first car really shown without an engine?**
Yes. The Lamborghini 350 GTV was displayed at the 1963 Turin Motor Show without an engine. The production 350 GT followed at Geneva in 1964, and 120 were built.

**Who sells more cars today, Ferrari or Lamborghini?**
In 2025 Lamborghini delivered 10,747 cars and Ferrari shipped 13,640.

### Sources

## EP 07: Porsche Bought a Nissan to Prove It Cheated. It Backfired.

URL: https://pistonorigins.com/episodes/nissan-gt-r-vs-porsche-911-turbo-nurburgring/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u6lgliMatSk
Published: 2026-10-21 · Length: 3:24 · Subject: Nissan GT-R R35

In 2008 Porsche bought a Nissan GT-R, flew it to Germany, lapped the Nürburgring and accused Nissan of cheating with race tyres. Nissan's reply: maybe Porsche's drivers needed lessons. This is the full GT-R vs Porsche 911 Turbo story. The R35 Nissan GT-R cost about half the price of a Porsche 911 Turbo, yet Nissan claimed a 7:29 Nordschleife lap, faster than Porsche's own GT2. Porsche's test came back at 7:54. Here's what Porsche said, what Nissan answered, and how Godzilla kept getting faster, all the way to the GT-R Nismo's 7:08.

### Key facts

- Car: Nissan GT-R (R35)
- Engine: VR38DETT 3.8 L twin-turbo V6, 480 PS
- Chief engineer: Kazutoshi Mizuno
- Nissan's claimed lap: 7:29, Nürburgring Nordschleife
- Porsche's test: GT-R 7:54 vs 911 Turbo 7:38 (2008)

### The story

#### The Porsche 911 Turbo and the everyday supercar

For years, if you wanted an everyday supercar, the default answer was the Porsche 911 Turbo. Then Nissan arrived with the R35 GT-R, a Japanese car costing roughly half as much. In the US, the 2009 GT-R was priced at $69,850, while the 2010 Porsche 911 Turbo started at $132,800.

In 2008 that gap turned into one of the stranger rows in car history. Porsche bought a Nissan GT-R, flew it to Germany, drove it around the Nürburgring and then suggested Nissan had cheated. Nissan's reply is still quoted today.


#### Godzilla and the hand-built VR38DETT engine

The GT-R's nickname, Godzilla, goes back to 1989, when Australian journalists at Wheels magazine first gave it to an earlier GT-R. The R35's chief engineer, Kazutoshi Mizuno, built the car around a hand-built twin-turbo V6, the 3.8-litre VR38DETT, rated at 480 PS.

Each engine is assembled by a single craftsman from start to finish, and that builder's name goes on a plaque on the engine. These engine builders are known as Takumi, and only nine people held that job. It was a deliberate signal that this was not simply a fast, cheap alternative to a Porsche but a carefully made machine in its own right.


#### Nissan's 7:29 Nürburgring Nordschleife lap

To prove the car, Nissan went where every manufacturer goes to make its point: the Nürburgring Nordschleife, around 20 km long with more than 150 corners. Test driver Toshio Suzuki set a lap of 7 minutes 29 seconds. Nissan said that was three seconds faster than Porsche's own 911 GT2.

A car at half the price beating Porsche on the track Porsche treats as home ground was always going to provoke a response from Stuttgart. The Nordschleife is where reputations are built, and a lap time quoted from it carries weight in showrooms and magazine pages alike. Nissan had not just claimed parity with the 911 Turbo; it had claimed to beat the more extreme GT2.


#### Porsche's test: GT-R 7:54 vs 911 Turbo 7:38

Porsche bought a US-specification GT-R for around $77,000, flew it to Germany and put its own drivers in it. Their best lap in the Nissan was 7:54, a full 25 seconds slower than Nissan's claim. Porsche's own 911 Turbo did 7:38 in the same test, and its GT2 went quicker still at 7:34.

Set those numbers side by side and the problem is obvious. In Porsche's hands, the GT-R was 16 seconds behind the 911 Turbo. In Nissan's hands, it was quicker than the GT2. Both could not be the whole story, and 25 seconds is a very large margin on a single lap, even one as long as the Nordschleife.

Porsche's conclusion was that Nissan must have run its record lap on special semi-slick race tyres. In other words, it was accusing Nissan of cheating. The head of the 911 programme, August Achleitner, tried to soften the blow, saying that the Nissan was a good car and that he did not want to say anything bad about it.


#### Nissan's reply: standard tyres and driving lessons

Nissan did not back down. Neil Reeve of Nissan Europe said the lap had been done on absolutely standard tyres available to customers in the showroom. Nissan offered to show Porsche the actual tyres and the video of the run.

Then came the line that made the story famous. In its statement, Nissan said any manufacturer buying a GT-R should follow the car's run-in procedure, and pointed out that it offers performance driving courses to GT-R owners. Nobody needed the subtext spelled out: perhaps Porsche's drivers were the ones who needed lessons.

It was an unusually sharp public exchange between two car makers. Manufacturers argue about lap times all the time, but rarely does one buy the other's car, publish its own numbers and imply foul play, and rarely does the other answer by questioning the rival's driving.


#### Who was right, Porsche or Nissan?

Porsche never proved that Nissan cheated, and Nissan never changed its story. What Nissan did instead was keep making the GT-R faster around the Nordschleife, with later laps of 7:26.70, 7:24.22 and 7:19.1.

The most emphatic answer came in 2013, when the GT-R Nismo, with Michael Krumm driving, lapped the Nordschleife in 7:08.679. Whatever happened with Porsche's own test car in 2008, the R35 had shown it could go far quicker than the 7:29 that started the argument.

The dispute still splits enthusiasts. Porsche's numbers came from a real car bought off the street, driven by its own people. Nissan's came from the company that built the car, on tyres it insisted anyone could buy. The two sides never settled it, and the GT-R's later lap times did most of Nissan's arguing for it.


### Questions and answers

**Did Porsche accuse Nissan of cheating with the GT-R?**
Yes. In 2008 Porsche bought a Nissan GT-R, lapped the Nürburgring in 7:54 against Nissan's claimed 7:29, and suggested Nissan had used race tyres. Nissan said the car used standard showroom tyres and suggested Porsche's drivers might benefit from a performance driving course.

**What is the fastest Nissan GT-R lap of the Nürburgring?**
The GT-R Nismo lapped the Nordschleife in 7:08.679 in 2013, driven by Michael Krumm.

## EP 06: Toyota Lost Money on Every Lexus LFA. Owners Didn't.

URL: https://pistonorigins.com/episodes/lexus-lfa-story/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NJSd2W415nA
Published: 2026-10-19 · Length: 4:22 · Subject: Lexus LFA

In 2010, Toyota sold the Lexus LFA for $375,000 and still lost money on every single one. Today one has sold for $1.81 million. Here's the full story of Toyota's craziest supercar. The 4.8-litre V10 built with Yamaha revved from idle to 9,000 rpm in 0.6 seconds, so fast that a needle couldn't keep up and Lexus fitted a digital rev counter. Toyota threw away five years of work on an aluminium car and started again in carbon fibre, tuned the engine's sound like a musical instrument, chased the Nürburgring, and built only 500 cars by hand.

### Key facts

- Engine: 1LR-GUE 4.8 L V10, developed with Yamaha
- Power: 552 hp
- Rev speed: Idle to 9,000 rpm in 0.6 seconds
- Built: 500 cars, Motomachi, Dec 2010 to Dec 2012
- Price new: $375,000

### The story

#### A $375,000 supercar that never paid for itself

In 2010, Toyota put a price of $375,000 on a car and, by the accounts of Car and Driver, still lost money on every single one it sold. That car was the Lexus LFA. It took around ten years to develop, only 500 were made, and in April 2026 one sold on Bring a Trailer for $1.81 million.

It is a strange story for a company known for being careful. Toyota built its fortune on sensible, profitable cars, yet here it was funding a hand-built V10 supercar that critics said cost too much and analysts said would never make a profit. To understand why, you have to go back to where the idea started.


#### How the Lexus LFA started: a bar in Hokkaido

The LFA story begins in 2000, in a bar in Hokkaido. A Toyota engineer named Haruhiko Tanahashi told his boss he wanted to build "the ultimate sports car". His boss did not laugh. He asked, "Why not?"

At the time Toyota was selling Camrys and Priuses, the kind of cars that pay the bills rather than set pulses racing. So the project began quietly, with a code name, TXS, and a tiny team. What happened next set the tone for the whole car: the first thing they perfected was not the body or the chassis, but the sound.


#### The Yamaha V10: 9,000 rpm and a digital rev counter

To build the engine, Toyota brought in Yamaha, a company that also makes pianos and motorcycles. Together they developed the 1LR-GUE, a 4.8-litre V10 that revved to 9,000 rpm and produced 552 hp.

The headline figure was not the power but the speed of the revs. The V10 could spin from idle to redline in 0.6 seconds. That was so quick that a conventional analogue needle physically could not keep up, so Lexus gave the LFA a digital tachometer instead. The engine had, quite literally, outrun the gauge.

Then the engineers tuned the engine like an instrument. The acoustic team studied a Formula One car at full revs, shaped the intake chamber after the body of a string instrument, and built three sound channels that carry the engine's voice directly into the cabin. Toyota's own engineers had a name for the result: "the roar of an angel".


#### From aluminium to carbon fibre: five years thrown away

By 2005 the car was close to finished, and then Toyota threw it away. The LFA had been engineered in aluminium, but Toyota's head of research, Kazuo Okamoto, had seen enough. His instruction, as reported, was blunt: "Get over it. Just go with carbon fiber."

Five years of work were scrapped. Toyota did not simply swap materials, either; it brought carbon fibre production in-house. The finished body was about 65% carbon fibre and roughly 100 kilos lighter than before. That saving came at a cost: the curing process limited the factory to about one car a day.


#### The Nürburgring, Hiromu Naruse and Akio Toyoda

From 2004, the LFA effectively lived at the Nürburgring, one of the most punishing circuits in the world. Its master test driver, Hiromu Naruse, shaped how the car drove, lap after lap on the Nordschleife.

The project reached the very top of the company. In 2009, Akio Toyoda, Toyota's future president, raced an LFA in the Nürburgring 24 Hours under an assumed name.

The development story also carries a tragedy. In June 2010, months before production began, Naruse was killed in a crash near the track while testing an LFA. He never saw the finished car, but the way every LFA drives owes a great deal to his work.


#### How many Lexus LFAs were made, and what they cost

Production ran from December 2010 to December 2012 at Toyota's Motomachi plant, where the cars were built by hand at a rate of about 20 a month. In total, 500 were made, each priced at $375,000.

The reaction was not kind. Critics said the LFA cost too much, analysts said it would never make a profit, and according to Car and Driver, Toyota lost money on every one. Then came the LFA Nürburgring Package, with more power, a fixed rear wing and a lap of the Nordschleife in 7 minutes 14.64 seconds in August 2011, one of the fastest times for a production car at that point.


#### Why Toyota built the LFA anyway

So why would the most careful car company on Earth build a car it knew would never pay for itself? Because the LFA was never really about profit. It taught Toyota how to work with carbon fibre, how to engineer sound, and how to build speed at the highest level. It also proved that Lexus could build a true supercar.

And there is a twist. Toyota may have lost money on every LFA, but the owners did not. A car that critics called overpriced at $375,000 has since changed hands for $1.81 million.


### Questions and answers

**Did Toyota lose money on the Lexus LFA?**
Yes. Toyota sold the Lexus LFA for $375,000 and still lost money on every one of the 500 cars it built by hand between 2010 and 2012. In April 2026 an LFA sold on Bring a Trailer for $1.81 million.

**Why does the Lexus LFA have a digital rev counter?**
Its 4.8-litre V10 could rev from idle to 9,000 rpm in 0.6 seconds, faster than a mechanical needle could follow, so Lexus fitted a digital rev counter.

**Why did the Lexus LFA switch from aluminium to carbon fibre?**
After about five years of development on an aluminium body, Toyota restarted the car in carbon-fibre-reinforced plastic to make it lighter and stiffer.

- 03:59 The twist

## EP 05: Why Ferrari FEARED This Honda | Honda NSX Story

URL: https://pistonorigins.com/episodes/honda-nsx-story/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LjII0wBnJHA
Published: 2026-10-14 · Length: 2:44 · Subject: Honda NSX (NA1)

The full Honda NSX (Acura NSX) history: how Ayrton Senna called Honda's secret supercar "fragile" at Suzuka in 1989, and how Honda answered with an aluminium body, a VTEC V6 and a chassis 50% stiffer, the car that woke up Ferrari. From the 1984 Pininfarina HP-X concept and the NS-X reveal at the 1989 Chicago Auto Show, to Senna's test, eight more months of Nürburgring development with Motoharu Kurosawa, the 3.0-litre C30A V6 with titanium connecting rods revving to 8,000 rpm, the hand-built cars from Tochigi, and what a $60,000 Acura NSX is worth today, this is the full NSX story.

### Key facts

- Engine: C30A 3.0 L VTEC V6, titanium connecting rods, 8,000 rpm
- Body: All-aluminium monocoque
- Revealed: 1989 Chicago Auto Show (as NS-X)
- Built: 1990–2005, Tochigi
- Price new (US): About $60,000 as the Acura NSX

### The story

#### Senna's verdict at Suzuka

Suzuka, 1989. The reigning Formula One world champion climbs out of Honda's secret new supercar and tells the engineers it is fragile. The driver was Ayrton Senna, then winning races in Honda-powered McLarens, and his verdict sent Honda back to work. Eight months later the car was 50% stiffer, and Ferrari had a problem.

That car became the original Honda NSX, the NA1, sold in America as the Acura NSX. Its promise sounds simple now, but at the time almost nobody believed it could be done: Ferrari speed with Honda reliability. Everyone said it could not be done. The story of how Honda did it runs from a Pininfarina concept car to a hand-built line in Tochigi, by way of the Nürburgring and a world champion's harsh verdict.


#### From the Pininfarina HP-X concept to the NS-X

The NSX story begins in 1984 with the HP-X, a concept car designed by Pininfarina. Five years later, in February 1989, the production-bound car was revealed at the Chicago Auto Show as the NS-X, short for New Sports Car Experimental.

Two things set it apart. The first was its body. The NSX was built from aluminium, with an all-aluminium monocoque, making it the first production car built this way. Compared with steel, the aluminium construction saved nearly 200 kilos.

The second was the cabin. The designers studied the cockpit of an F-16 fighter jet and borrowed its thinking: the cabin was pushed forward, with glass all around.


#### Eight months to fix "fragile": Senna and the Nürburgring

Then Honda handed a prototype to the one driver who would notice every flaw. Between Formula One sessions at Suzuka, Senna drove the NSX and called it fragile. For a company whose engines were powering his championship-winning McLaren, that was not a comment to ignore.

Honda spent another eight months developing the car. Part of that work happened at the Nürburgring, where test driver Motoharu Kurosawa reported every flex in the chassis and engineers hand-welded new braces to cure it. By the end, the structure was around 50% stiffer than the one Senna had criticised.


#### The C30A VTEC V6 and the Tochigi factory

The engine changed late in development too. The 3.0-litre V6, known as the C30A, was redesigned to use VTEC. It was also fitted with titanium connecting rods, a first for a production car, and it revved to 8,000 rpm.

How the NSX was built mattered as much as what went into it. Every car was assembled in Tochigi by a team of about 200 hand-picked technicians, each with at least ten years of experience.


#### The Acura NSX in America and Gordon Murray's verdict

In November 1990 the car arrived in the United States as the Acura NSX, priced at around $60,000. It handled like a race car and started every morning like a Honda, which was exactly the point. Ferrari speed and Honda reliability had been treated as opposites; the NSX put them in the same car.

Its influence reached well beyond its sales. Gordon Murray, the designer of the McLaren F1, called it a landmark car, one that woke up not only a lazy Ferrari but Porsche as well. Honda kept building the first-generation NSX for 15 years, from 1990 until 2005, and made just over 18,000 cars in that time.


#### What an original Honda NSX is worth today

The $60,000 Acura has aged well as an investment. Clean examples now sell for roughly $80,000 to $120,000, and one low-mileage 1991 car sold at auction for $155,911.

Senna called it fragile, and Honda answered by turning it into the supercar that changed supercars. Its lasting lesson is a simple one: the best supercar might be the one you can drive every day.


### Questions and answers

**What did Ayrton Senna say about the Honda NSX?**
Testing a prototype at Suzuka in 1989, Ayrton Senna called the NSX "fragile". Honda spent about eight more months developing the car, including at the Nürburgring, and made the chassis around 50% stiffer.

**What engine does the original Honda NSX have?**
The C30A, a 3.0-litre V6 with VTEC and titanium connecting rods that revs to 8,000 rpm.

**How much is an original Honda NSX worth?**
The Acura NSX cost about $60,000 new. Good examples now trade around $80,000 to $120,000, and one sold at auction for $155,911.

## EP 04: The AE86 Wasn't Fast. So Why Is It a Legend?

URL: https://pistonorigins.com/episodes/toyota-ae86-story/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=flQ66uxn0DM
Published: 2026-10-12 · Length: 5:08 · Subject: Toyota AE86 Corolla

The full Toyota AE86 history: how a slow, cheap 1983 Corolla became the Hachi-Roku legend behind Initial D and drifting. It was never fast, so why does everyone still want one? From Toyota keeping rear-wheel drive when the rest of the Corolla range went front-wheel drive, to the 4A-GE twin-cam that loved to rev, the $11,530 Corolla GT-S, Keiichi Tsuchiya "the Drift King", Initial D and the "Takumi tax", all the way to the 2012 Toyota 86, this is the full AE86 story.

### Key facts

- Car: Toyota Corolla Levin / Sprinter Trueno (AE86)
- Engine: 4A-GE 1.6 L twin-cam inline-four
- Layout: Front engine, rear-wheel drive
- 0–60 mph: 9.5 s (Car and Driver, Corolla GT-S)
- US price, 1985: $11,530 (Corolla GT-S)

### The story

#### A cheap Corolla that became a legend

In 1983, Toyota sold a cheap, boxy little Corolla and, almost by accident, built a legend. It was light, it was rear-wheel drive, and it had a twin-cam engine that loved to rev. It would go on to help start a whole motorsport.

That car was the Toyota AE86. It was never fast in a straight line, and it was never meant to be special. Yet it became a legend, and the reasons say a lot about what makes a car great to drive.


#### The last rear-wheel-drive Corolla: Levin and Trueno

To understand the AE86, you have to understand the moment it was born. By 1983, front-wheel drive was taking over. It was cheaper to build, roomier inside and easier to drive in the rain. So Toyota moved its new Corolla to the front wheels.

The sporty coupes did not follow. The Corolla Levin and the Sprinter Trueno stayed on the older platform, with the engine in the front and power going to the back. In other words, the old car was the one that kept rear-wheel drive, and that turned out to matter enormously.

The two were essentially one car with two faces. The Levin had fixed headlights, while the Trueno had pop-up headlights.


#### Why the AE86 is called Hachi-Roku

Inside Toyota, the car was known by its chassis code, AE86. In Japan, people shortened that to Hachi-Roku, Japanese for "eight-six". Two badges, two faces, one nickname.


#### The 4A-GE engine: 1.6 litres that loved to rev

Under the bonnet sat the AE86's real secret, the 4A-GE. It was a 1.6-litre inline-four with twin cams and 16 valves, making about 130 horsepower in Japan and just 112 in America.

On paper, that is not fast. But the AE86 was light, balanced and eager. The sportiest versions weighed around 900 kilos, less than a ton, and the 4A-GE kept pulling all the way to 7,500 rpm. The whole car felt alive in the driver's hands.

In America it arrived as the Corolla GT-S, and it was priced like what it was, an economy car. In 1985 you could buy one new for $11,530. Most buyers walked straight past it. A few did not.


#### Was the AE86 actually fast?

Mostly, no. In a straight line plenty of ordinary family cars would beat it. Car and Driver timed the Corolla GT-S at 9.5 seconds from 0 to 60 mph, hardly the figure of a performance legend.

So how did it beat faster cars on a mountain road? It was fast where it counted, in the corners. Low weight, rear-wheel drive and an engine that rewarded high revs meant a skilled driver could carry speed through a bend that more powerful cars could not match.


#### Keiichi Tsuchiya, the Drift King

That brings the story to the mountains of Japan and a young driver named Keiichi Tsuchiya. He learned his craft on the touge, the twisting mountain passes, throwing his car sideways through corners at speeds that made no sense.

His street driving videos made him famous and got him into serious trouble with the racing authorities; he nearly lost his licence. He also became known as the Drift King. Tsuchiya went on to race the AE86 in the All-Japan Touring Car Championship, finished second overall at Le Mans in 1999, and helped turn drifting from a street habit into a real motorsport.


#### Initial D, the Takumi tax and the Toyota 86

Then, in 1995, a manga changed everything. Initial D, by Shuichi Shigeno, told the story of a teenage tofu delivery driver who wins downhill races in his father's white and black Sprinter Trueno. Tsuchiya even worked on the anime as a consultant. A tofu delivery car beating supercars was an idea a whole generation fell in love with.

Fans have a name for what happened to prices next: the Takumi tax, after the story's hero. A 1985 Corolla GT-S that cost $11,530 new sold at auction in 2021 for $40,000. For a Corolla, that sounds absurd, but once you know the story it makes sense.

Toyota noticed. In 2012 it launched a brand-new rear-wheel-drive coupe, built with Subaru and sold alongside the Subaru BRZ, and named it simply the 86. Light, balanced and affordable, it was a direct nod to the Hachi-Roku.

The AE86 endures because it proved power is not everything. A boxy little Corolla that was never meant to be special taught the world to drive sideways.


### Questions and answers

**Was the Toyota AE86 actually fast?**
No. Car and Driver measured the Corolla GT-S at 9.5 seconds from 0 to 60 mph. Its legend comes from its light, rear-wheel-drive balance and the rev-happy 4A-GE engine, which made it ideal for drifting.

**Why is the AE86 called Hachi-Roku?**
Hachi-roku is Japanese for "eight-six", from the car's AE86 chassis code.

**What is the "Takumi tax"?**
The price premium on AE86s caused by Initial D, whose hero Takumi drives one. A Corolla GT-S that cost $11,530 new in 1985 sold for $40,000 at auction in 2021.

- 00:29 A Corolla out of time
- 01:17 The heart: 4A-GE
- 02:00 Cheap thrills: the Corolla GT-S

- 02:48 Keiichi Tsuchiya, the Drift King

## EP 03: Mazda's Rotary Engine Should Never Have Worked (RX-7 & 787B Story)

URL: https://pistonorigins.com/episodes/mazda-rotary-engine-rx-7-787b-story/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R9jLpyg8-3A
Published: 2026-10-06 · Length: 6:24 · Subject: Mazda RX-7 and 787B

The Mazda rotary engine has no pistons. It drinks fuel, burns oil, and nearly bankrupted Mazda, yet it won Le Mans with the 787B and powered the RX-7. So why do people love the rotary so much? From a 1961 license deal with NSU to the "devil's nail marks" on early engines, the Cosmo Sport and the 84-hour Nürburgring marathon, the 1973 oil crisis, the RX-7, the 787B's 1991 Le Mans win, the FD RX-7 and the rotary's 2023 comeback in the MX-30 R-EV, this is the full Mazda rotary story.

### Key facts

- Engine type: Wankel rotary (no pistons)
- Licence: From NSU, 1961
- Le Mans: Won in 1991 with the four-rotor 787B (R26B)
- FD RX-7: 13B-REW twin-rotor, sequential twin-turbo
- Comeback: 2023, as a range extender in the MX-30 R-EV

### The story

#### An engine with no pistons

The Mazda rotary engine has no pistons. It drinks fuel, it burns oil, and it nearly bankrupted the company that built it. It also won the world's most famous race on what was very nearly its last chance, powered the RX-7, and in 2023 Mazda brought it back from the dead. For a channel called Piston Origins, it is an odd choice of hero, but few engines have a better story.

It begins in Hiroshima in 1961. Mazda, still trading under its earlier company name, was a small firm that mostly built trucks. Its president wanted something no other car maker had, and he found it in Germany: a strange engine invented by Felix Wankel, which Mazda licensed from NSU.


#### How a Wankel rotary engine works

Instead of pistons pumping up and down, a Wankel rotary uses a triangle-shaped rotor spinning inside an oval housing. Intake, compression, power and exhaust all happen in one smooth rotation. That gives the rotary fewer moving parts, a tiny package and an appetite for revs.

The size matters as much as the smoothness. A rotary is so compact that it can sit low and far back in the car, which is excellent for handling. On paper it sounded perfect. There was just one problem: it kept destroying itself.


#### The devil's nail marks and the apex seal fix

After only hours of running, the rotor's tips, known as the apex seals, chattered against the housing and carved scratches into its surface. Mazda's engineers had a name for them: the devil's nail marks.

Mazda handed the problem to a team of 47 young engineers led by Kenichi Yamamoto. In 1963 they tried a seal with cross-shaped holes. Then came a new material, an aluminium-carbon composite developed with an outside partner. The scratches stopped. In a very real sense, the whole programme was saved by a tiny seal.


#### Cosmo Sport and the 84-hour Nürburgring marathon

On 30 May 1967 Mazda launched the Cosmo Sport, the world's first mass-production car with a two-rotor engine. Buyers still didn't trust the technology, so Mazda went looking for proof. In 1968 it entered an 84-hour non-stop marathon at the Nürburgring. One Cosmo finished fourth overall out of 59 cars, after covering more than 9,700 km.

Then came 1973 and the oil crisis. A US government report criticised the rotary's fuel economy, and over the next three years Mazda's sales fell 53 per cent, with rotary sales down 83 per cent. The company came close to bankruptcy. Most manufacturers would have killed the engine there and then. Mazda doubled down instead: Yamamoto's team went back to work and doubled the rotary's fuel economy in three years.


#### The Mazda RX-7 and the rebuild myth

In 1978 Mazda bet on a small, light sports car: the RX-7. It sold more than 140,000 cars in its first two years.

The RX-7 also carries a reputation that still follows every rotary: that it needs a rebuild every 50,000 miles. The truth sits in the middle. Rotaries burn a little oil by design, and the apex seals remain the weak point, so an engine that runs low on oil or is never revved can wear out early. Looked after properly, many go much further. The channel's verdict is "mostly myth", with a firm reminder to rotary owners to check their oil.


#### Mazda 787B: the 1991 Le Mans win

The moment rotary fans still talk about came at Le Mans in 1991. New rules were about to end the rotary's racing career there for good, but they were delayed by one year, giving Mazda one last chance with the 787B. It used four rotors, made around 700 horsepower and screamed to 9,000 rpm.

On 23 June 1991, car number 55, with Johnny Herbert at the wheel, crossed the line after 362 laps. Mazda had won. It was the first Japanese manufacturer ever to win Le Mans outright, and it remains the only winner with a rotary engine. After that, the rotary was gone from Le Mans for ever.


#### The FD RX-7 and the 13B-REW

On the road, the rotary built its masterpiece in 1992: the third-generation RX-7, known as the FD. It used a twin-rotor 13B-REW with sequential twin turbos, one working at low revs and the second joining in at around 4,500 rpm. It made 255 horsepower in America, weighed about 1,300 kg, and wore a shape many still call one of the most beautiful of the 1990s.

The FD became a pop-culture icon too. In the anime Initial D, one of the main rivals drives a yellow FD. In Tokyo Drift, Han's orange and black RX-7 became one of the best-known movie cars of the 2000s. And in Gran Turismo, a whole generation learned what a rotary sounds like at full song.


#### Why the rotary went silent, and the 2023 comeback

Popularity didn't save it in the showroom. By 1995 the FD cost nearly $38,000, and few mechanics understood rotaries. Mazda pulled it from America after 1995, with only around 14,000 sold there. In Japan the RX-7 lived on until 2002, and the RX-8 carried the rotary until 2012. Then the engine went silent. Today a really clean FD can be worth more than $50,000, more than it cost new.

Mazda never let go, though. On 22 June 2023 rotary production restarted in Hiroshima, this time with the engine working as a range-extending generator in the MX-30 R-EV. So why do people love an engine that drinks fuel and burns oil? Because it was never supposed to work, and Mazda made it work anyway.


### Questions and answers

**How does a rotary engine work without pistons?**
A Wankel rotary engine uses a triangular rotor spinning inside an oval-like housing. As it turns, the three chambers between the rotor and the housing take in, compress, ignite and exhaust the fuel mixture, so there are no pistons, connecting rods or valves.

**When did Mazda win Le Mans?**
Mazda won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1991 with the four-rotor 787B.

**Is the Mazda rotary engine still made?**
Yes. Mazda restarted rotary production in 2023, using it as a range-extending generator in the MX-30 R-EV.

## EP 02: Why the Nissan Skyline GT-R R34 Was Banned in America (Godzilla's Full Story)

URL: https://pistonorigins.com/episodes/nissan-skyline-gt-r-r34-banned-in-america/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_QTVeqC9ARM
Published: 2026-10-05 · Length: 3:42 · Subject: Nissan Skyline GT-R R34

Why was the Nissan Skyline GT-R R34 banned in the USA, and is the R34 finally legal to import in 2026? For 25 years Americans could only drive Godzilla in Gran Turismo. This is the complete R34 GT-R history: from the 1969 Hakosuka to the R32 that earned the "Godzilla" nickname, the RB26DETT twin-turbo engine, the 25-year import rule and the $1.357 million Paul Walker R34 auction. In this episode of Piston Origins:

### Key facts

- Engine: RB26DETT 2.6 L twin-turbo inline-six
- Official output: 276 hp ("gentlemen's agreement")
- Drivetrain: ATTESA E-TS Pro AWD, Getrag 6-speed
- Revealed: 8 January 1999
- Built: 11,578 (1999–2002)

### The story

#### The car Americans could only drive in a video game

For 25 years, most Americans could only drive the Nissan Skyline GT-R R34 in a video game. Import one the wrong way and the government could take it away. Today it is one of the most wanted cars on Earth, and the reason starts long before the R34 itself, with the car that first carried the GT-R badge.


#### The Hakosuka: where the Skyline GT-R began

The story starts in 1969. Prince had just merged with Nissan, and its engineers dropped a racing six into a boxy family saloon. They called it the GT-R, for Gran Turismo Racing. Officially it was the Skyline 2000GT-R, chassis code PGC10, but fans called it the Hakosuka, the "box Skyline", and it dominated Japanese racing.

Then the oil crisis hit. The second-generation GT-R lasted for just 197 cars, and the name went quiet for 16 years.


#### The R32 GT-R and the Godzilla nickname

In 1989 the GT-R came back with a vengeance. The R32 GT-R had a twin-turbo six and clever all-wheel drive, and it crushed everything on the track. In Australia it won so much in touring-car racing that Wheels magazine gave it a nickname: Godzilla, the monster from Japan. So one of the best-known names in Japanese performance cars was, in fact, an Australian idea.


#### The R34 GT-R reveal: shorter, stiffer, sharper

On 8 January 1999 Nissan revealed the R34. The brief can be summed up in three words: shorter, stiffer, sharper. The body was around 56 per cent stiffer than the R33's, and the wheelbase was cut by 55 mm.

What made the R34 feel so far ahead of its time was the technology packed around the driver. It used ATTESA E-TS Pro all-wheel drive with an active differential, Super-HICAS four-wheel steering and a Getrag six-speed gearbox. In the dash sat a 5.8-inch multi-function display showing boost and temperatures, in 1999. The R34 was a computer on wheels, and it felt as if it had driven straight out of Gran Turismo.


#### The RB26DETT engine and the 276 hp gentlemen's agreement

Under the bonnet sat the legendary RB26DETT: 2.6 litres, six cylinders in a row and two turbochargers. Officially it made 276 hp (280 PS), the figure set by the same gentlemen's agreement between Japanese car makers that capped the Toyota Supra. Tested cars, however, made closer to 330. And tuners took the RB26 way, way past that, which is a large part of why the engine's reputation has outlived the car's production run.


#### Why the R34 GT-R couldn't be sold in the US

Gran Turismo is exactly where most Americans met the R34, because in America you couldn't buy one. The car was never built to US federal safety rules, the FMVSS standards, so it could not be sold or imported new. One California importer, Motorex, found a workaround in the early 2000s, until regulators shut it down.

That left a whole generation to fall in love with the car on a PlayStation, and in 2 Fast 2 Furious, where Paul Walker drove a silver and blue R34. The forbidden-fruit status only made the Skyline more desirable: a car you could race every evening on a console, but never park on your own drive.


#### Production numbers, the V-Spec II Nür and the $1.357 million auction

Only 11,578 R34 GT-Rs were built before production ended in 2002. The rarest of them, the Nür editions such as the V-Spec II Nür, number only in the hundreds.

That scarcity, combined with the car's film history, has pushed prices to extraordinary levels. In 2023 an R34 from the Fast and Furious films, customised for Paul Walker, sold at auction for $1.357 million. More than a million dollars, for a Skyline.


#### The 25-year rule: Godzilla comes to America

After all that waiting, the R34 is finally becoming legal in America. Under the 25-year import rule, each car becomes eligible 25 years after the month it was built. The first, early-1999 cars crossed that line in 2024, and because production ran until 2002, more R34s become eligible as each build month passes.

For the generation that grew up with it on a screen, that means the car regulators once kept out can now arrive legally, one build month at a time. Godzilla is coming to America at last.


### Questions and answers

**Why was the Nissan Skyline GT-R R34 banned in the USA?**
It was never certified to US federal safety and emissions standards (FMVSS), so it could not be legally sold or imported new. Apart from a small number brought in through the Motorex loophole, Americans had to wait for the 25-year import rule.

**Is the R34 GT-R legal in the US?**
Under the 25-year rule, each R34 becomes eligible for import 25 years after its build month. The first cars (early 1999 builds) became eligible in 2024, and production ran to 2002.

**How many R34 GT-Rs were made?**
11,578, between 1999 and 2002.

**Why is the Nissan GT-R called Godzilla?**
Australia's Wheels magazine nicknamed the R32 GT-R "Godzilla", the monster from Japan, after it dominated Australian touring-car racing.

- 0:55 The R32 and the Godzilla nickname

- 2:30 Why Americans couldn't buy one
- 2:50 Rarity and the $1.357M auction
- 3:14 Godzilla comes to America

- Facts from Nissan, Wikipedia, State of Speed and Bonhams auction results.

## EP 01: The Toyota Supra Mk4: How Toyota Built a Legend

URL: https://pistonorigins.com/episodes/toyota-supra-mk4-story/
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=18hr_2O-4cg
Published: 2026-10-04 · Length: 3:34 · Subject: Toyota Supra Mk4 (A80)

How did a Japanese sports coupe from 1993 become one of the most wanted cars on the planet? From the 1967 Toyota 2000GT to the first Celica Supra, chief engineer Isao Tsuzuki's "less is more" Mk4, and the legendary 2JZ-GTE with its sequential twin turbos, this is the full story of the A80 Toyota Supra.

### Key facts

- Engine: 2JZ-GTE 3.0 L sequential twin-turbo inline-six
- Chief engineer: Isao Tsuzuki
- Philosophy: "Less is more": weight saved everywhere
- Launched: 1993
- Ancestor: 1967 Toyota 2000GT

### The story

#### The Mk4 Supra: a legend more than 30 years on

Some cars are fast. Some cars are famous. And then there is the one people still call the legend. Toyota built the Mk4 Supra, the A80, more than 30 years ago, and tuners are still pushing it past 1,000 horsepower. How did a Japanese sports coupé from 1993 become one of the most wanted cars on the planet? To understand it, you have to go back to the cars that came before.


#### Where the Supra name came from: the 2000GT and the Celica Supra

In 1967 Toyota built the 2000GT, a long-nosed beauty that proved a Japanese company could build a world-class sports car. It is the Supra's spiritual ancestor, and its influence would show up again decades later.

Then, in 1978, Toyota took its Celica, stretched the nose, dropped in a straight-six and gave it a new name: Supra. It is Latin for "above", or "to go beyond". By 1986 the Supra stood on its own, with a turbocharged 3-litre straight-six. But Toyota wanted something more.


#### Building the A80: Isao Tsuzuki's "less is more"

In February 1989 work began on the fourth-generation Supra, led by chief engineer Isao Tsuzuki, who had already worked on the first Celica and the MR2. His rule was simple: less is more. The new car had to be shorter, lower, wider and lighter, even while carrying more safety equipment.

So the team went to war on weight. The Mk4 got an aluminium bonnet, aluminium suspension arms, a plastic fuel tank and a magnesium steering-wheel frame. They even used hollow fibres in the carpet. Every gram counted, and the finished car was about 100 kg lighter than the one it replaced.

The shape followed the same thinking. Its flowing lines owed more to the 2000GT of the 1960s than to the boxy Supra that came immediately before it, which is why the A80 still looks so different from its predecessor.


#### The 1993 launch: targa roof, hoop wing and huge brakes

The new Supra debuted at the Chicago Auto Show in 1993, and car lovers fell for the details. There was that huge hoop wing, a removable targa roof and double-wishbone suspension at all four corners. The brakes were so good that Car and Driver stopped one from 70 mph in just 149 feet. Zero to 60 mph took about four and a half seconds.

Those numbers made the Supra a serious performance car straight out of the box. But the reason it became a legend sits under the bonnet.


#### The 2JZ-GTE engine and its sequential twin turbos

The heart of the Mk4 Supra Turbo is the 2JZ-GTE: 3 litres, six cylinders in a row, a cast-iron block and two turbochargers developed with Hitachi. The clever part is that they work in sequence. Low in the rev range, one turbo does the work so the engine responds quickly. Higher up, the second joins in for the big rush.

In Japan the engine was rated at 280 PS (about 276 hp), the ceiling set by a gentlemen's agreement between car makers. In America it was rated at 320 hp. Power went through Toyota's first six-speed manual gearbox, developed with Getrag.

That iron block was so overbuilt that tuners doubled the factory power on standard internals, and the wildest builds have gone past 1,000 horsepower. It is the main reason the 2JZ name still carries so much weight in tuning circles.


#### Tuners, Hollywood and The Fast and the Furious

The tuning world had already discovered the Supra when, in 2001, an orange Supra in The Fast and the Furious turned it into a superstar. A car already loved in tuner circles was now famous far beyond them.

Its value followed. One of the cars from that film sold at auction in 2021 for $550,000. For a Supra.


#### The legacy of the Toyota Supra Mk4

Sales of the A80 ended in America in 1998 and in Japan in 2002. But the Mk4 never really left. A light, carefully engineered body, an engine built far stronger than it needed to be and a starring role on screen combined to keep it at the top of enthusiasts' wish lists.

More than 30 years after Tsuzuki's team started cutting grams, it is still the car people dream about.


### Questions and answers

**What engine is in the Mk4 Toyota Supra?**
The Mk4 (A80) Supra Turbo uses the 2JZ-GTE, a 3.0-litre inline-six with sequential twin turbochargers, famous for handling huge power with modest upgrades.

**Who designed the Mk4 Toyota Supra?**
Chief engineer Isao Tsuzuki led the A80 Supra with a "less is more" philosophy, cutting weight wherever possible.

**Why is the Mk4 Supra so expensive?**
Its tuning potential, the 2JZ-GTE engine and its role in Hollywood and tuner culture made the A80 Supra one of the most wanted Japanese cars. One sold for $550,000.

- 0:20 Where the Supra name came from
- 0:52 Building the Mk4: less is more
- 1:44 The launch and what fans love
- 2:08 The 2JZ-GTE engine
- 2:42 Tuners and Hollywood

## FAQ

**What is Piston Origins?**
Piston Origins is a car-history channel on YouTube. Each full episode tells the origin story of one legendary car, such as the Toyota Supra Mk4, Nissan Skyline GT-R R34, Mazda RX-7, Honda NSX or Toyota AE86, and each 60-second Short reveals one little-known fact about a car or engine.

**Who presents Piston Origins? Is the host real?**
The host, Skye, and the narration voice are AI-generated. The research, facts and sources are real, and every source is listed in the video description and on the episode page on this site.

**How often does Piston Origins post new videos?**
A new full car story every week, plus 60-second car secrets in YouTube Shorts.

**Where do Piston Origins' facts come from?**
Each episode is written from a reference sheet in which every fact has a source: manufacturer press material, magazines such as Car and Driver, Top Gear and Hagerty, auction results and reference works. Those sources are listed on each episode page. Anything that cannot be sourced is cut or softened.

**Which cars has Piston Origins covered?**
Toyota Supra Mk4, Nissan Skyline GT-R R34, Mazda RX-7 and 787B, Toyota AE86, Honda NSX, Lexus LFA, Nissan GT-R R35, Toyota Celica GT-Four ST205, and the Ferrari vs Lamborghini rivalry.

**Can I suggest a car for Piston Origins to cover?**
Yes. Leave a comment on any Piston Origins video on YouTube or send a message on Instagram (@pistonorigins). Topics are picked from the comments.
